facts.title: Born from two youth clubs
facts.body: Charlton Athletic were formed on 9 June 1905 when a group of boys from the East Street Mission and Blundell Mission youth clubs in Charlton, south-east London, merged their teams. The club turned professional in 1920 and joined the Football League a year later.

facts.title: The one year they weren't at The Valley
facts.body: Charlton first played at The Valley in 1919, but in 1923 the club moved to The Mount in Catford as part of a proposed merger with Catford Southend. The merger fell through within a year and Charlton moved straight back to SE7.

facts.title: Where the name 'Addicks' comes from
facts.body: The most widely told explanation is that a local fishmonger who sponsored the club used to give the players haddock suppers after matches — 'haddock' warped in local slang into 'Addicks', and it stuck.

facts.title: Two promotions in a row — a Football League first
facts.body: Charlton won the Third Division South title in 1934–35 and were runners-up in the Second Division the very next season, reaching the First Division for the first time in the club's history. They were the first side ever to go from the Third Division to the First Division in successive seasons.

facts.title: Runners-up in the top flight — still the club's best finish
facts.body: In 1936–37, their first full season in the top flight, Charlton finished second in the First Division, just three points behind champions Manchester City. Nearly 90 years on, it remains Charlton's highest-ever league finish.

facts.title: The Valley's biggest ever crowd
facts.body: 75,031 people packed into The Valley on 12 February 1938 for an FA Cup fifth-round tie against Aston Villa, which finished 1-1. It's still the record attendance for the ground and one of the largest crowds ever recorded outside England's top two divisions.

facts.title: A goalkeeper found after tragedy
facts.body: In 1934, Charlton's keeper Alex Wright was killed in a freak accident, breaking his neck diving into the sea with teammates in Torquay. Within two weeks manager Jimmy Seed had signed Sam Bartram — who went on to make a club-record 623 appearances over 22 years, a number nobody has come close to since.

facts.title: Runners-up, then champions
facts.body: Charlton lost the 1946 FA Cup final to Derby County, then went straight back to Wembley the following year and beat Burnley 1-0 after extra time to win the only major trophy in the club's history.

facts.title: The trophy was handed over by a future US President
facts.body: Guest of honour at the 1947 FA Cup final was General Dwight D. Eisenhower — five years before he was elected President of the United States. He presented the cup to Charlton captain Don Welsh on the Wembley steps.

facts.title: 7-6, down to ten men
facts.body: In December 1957 Charlton beat Huddersfield Town 7-6 at The Valley after captain Derek Ufton dislocated his shoulder just 17 minutes in. With no substitutes allowed in that era, ten men fought back from behind to win one of English football's most remarkable matches.

facts.title: 101 points — the highest total in club history
facts.body: Chris Powell's side won the 2011–12 League One title with 101 points, still Charlton's best-ever points haul in a single season.

facts.title: Record win: 8-0
facts.body: Charlton's biggest ever victory came in 2019, thrashing Stevenage 8-0. Derek Hales remains the club's all-time record goalscorer with 168 goals across his two spells.

facts.title: Four spells in the top flight
facts.body: Charlton have played in England's top division in four separate eras: 1936–1957, 1986–1990, 1998–1999, and 2000–2007 — a Premier League ever-present for seven straight seasons in that last spell.

facts.title: Charlton fans formed an actual political party
facts.body: Forced out of The Valley in 1985 amid a battle over the ground's freehold, Charlton spent seven years ground-sharing at Crystal Palace's Selhurst Park and West Ham's Upton Park. When Greenwich Council rejected plans for the club to return home, supporters founded 'The Valley Party' and contested all 36 wards of the 1990 local elections on a single issue: bring Charlton home.

facts.title: 14,838 votes — and the council backed down
facts.body: The Valley Party won no seats, but took 10.9% of the vote across Greenwich, enough to force the council back to the negotiating table. Charlton finally returned to The Valley on 5 December 1992, beating Portsmouth 1-0 in front of 8,337 emotional fans.
